method_card.title: Hooke's Law and Elastic PE
method_card.content:
Two equations. Hooke's law \(F = ke\): force (N) = spring constant (N/m) × extension (m). Elastic PE \(E_{pe} = \frac{1}{2}ke^2\): energy (J) stored in a stretched or compressed spring.

Keep the extension in metres, and remember it is the change in length, not the total length. Check whether your board gives you the \(E_{pe}\) equation or expects you to recall it.

steps: Gold problems link two ideas: a spring's energy converts into movement, or comes from a drop.
Launch: all the stored \(E_{pe} = \frac{1}{2}ke^2\) becomes \(E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2\). Set them equal, solve for v.
Drop onto a spring: the lost \(E_p = mgh\) becomes elastic PE. Work out the energy first, then the quantity asked for.
gold.title: Gold: chain two equations

example.question: A spring (k = 100 N/m) stretched 0.20 m launches a 0.50 kg trolley. Find its speed, assuming all Epe becomes KE.

steps: Bronze problems give two of the three quantities in \(F = ke\): force in N, spring constant k in N/m, extension e in m.
Substitute straight in, or rearrange first: \(k = F/e\) for stiffness, \(e = F/k\) for extension.
Keep the extension in metres. Here the lengths are already in metres.
bronze.title: Bronze: one equation, one step

example.question: A spring of spring constant 80 N/m is stretched by 0.05 m. Calculate the force.

steps: Silver adds one twist: either the length is in centimetres (divide by 100 for metres) or you must rearrange before substituting.
For elastic PE use \(E_{pe} = \frac{1}{2}ke^2\): square the extension first, then multiply by k, then halve.
To find e from energy, rearrange: \(e = \sqrt{2E_{pe}/k}\), taking the square root last.

gold.question: A spring (k = 400 N/m) is compressed by 12 cm and releases a 0.16 kg ball. Assuming all elastic PE converts to kinetic energy, calculate the ball's speed in m/s.

guided_steps.say: Elastic PE launches the ball as kinetic energy: \(E_{pe} = \frac{1}{2}ke^2\) then \(E_{pe} = \frac{1}{2}mv^2\).

guided_steps.pre: All 2.88 J becomes KE. First work out ½ × 0.16 =

guided_steps.done: Back to 2.88 J, so v = 6.0 m/s is right.

misconceptions.message: Epe = ½ × 400 × 0.12² = 2.88 J. Then 2.88 = ½ × 0.16 × v², so v² = 36 and v = 6.0 m/s. 2.88 is the energy, not the speed.
After v² = 36 take the square root: v = 6.0 m/s, not 36.

guided_steps.say: Rearrange \(E_{pe} = \frac{1}{2}ke^2\) for k: \(k = 2E_{pe}/e^2\). Find the extension first.

guided_steps.hint: Double the energy, then divide by e².

guided_steps.done: Back to 0.450 J, so k = 250 N/m is right.
guided_steps.hint: ½ × 250 × e² gives the stored energy.

misconceptions.message: Extension = 30 − 24 = 6 cm = 0.06 m. k = 2 × 0.450 ÷ 0.06² = 250 N/m. Using the total 30 cm (0.30 m) gives 10 N/m.
Square the extension in the formula: k = 2 × 0.450 ÷ 0.06². Forgetting to square gives 0.9 ÷ 0.06 = 15 N/m.

guided_steps.say: At maximum compression all the gravitational PE has become elastic PE, so first find \(E_p = mgh\).

guided_steps.pre: Mass and height are in base units. GPE = m × g × h = 0.20 × 9.8 × 3.0. First 0.20 × 9.8 =
This equals the elastic PE stored. Check: 5.88 ÷ 3.0 =
guided_steps.done: 1.96 N is the ball's weight (0.20 × 9.8), so Epe = 5.88 J is right.

misconceptions.message: Use g = 9.8 N/kg: Epe = 0.20 × 9.8 × 3.0 = 5.88 J. Using g = 10 gives 6.0 J.

gold.display: Two springs A and B are connected end-to-end (in series). Spring A has k = 100 N/m and spring B has k = 200 N/m. A force of 10 N is applied. In series the same force acts on each spring. Calculate the total extension of the pair, in metres.
gold.question: Two springs A and B are connected end-to-end (in series). Spring A has k = 100 N/m and spring B has k = 200 N/m. A force of 10 N is applied. In series the same force acts on each spring. Calculate the total extension of the pair, in metres.

guided_steps.say: In series the same 10 N acts on both springs. Find each extension with \(e = F/k\), then add them.

guided_steps.done: The same 10 N acts on each, so the total extension 0.15 m is right.
guided_steps.hint: k × e for B returns the 10 N force.

misconceptions.message: The same 10 N acts on each spring. eA = 10 ÷ 100 = 0.10 m, eB = 10 ÷ 200 = 0.05 m, total = 0.15 m. 0.10 m is only spring A.
In series you add the extensions, not the spring constants. 10 ÷ (100 + 200) = 0.033 m is the wrong route.

guided_steps.pre: The extension is in metres: e = 0.04 m. Square it: 0.04² =

silver.display: A spring (k = 300 N/m) has 5.4 J of elastic potential energy stored in it. Calculate the extension.
silver.question: A spring (k = 300 N/m) has 5.4 J of elastic potential energy stored in it. Calculate the extension.

guided_steps.hint: Double the energy, then divide by k.
Take the square root; give 4 significant figures.

guided_steps.done: Back to 5.4 J, so e = 0.1897 m is right.

misconceptions.message: e² = 2 × 5.4 ÷ 300 = 0.036. Take the square root: e = 0.190 m. Stopping at 0.036 forgets the root.
Use the ½: e² = 2 × 5.4 ÷ 300 = 0.036. Dropping the doubling gives e² = 0.018 and e = 0.134 m.

silver.hint: Find the energy in one spring, then double it for both.
silver.display: Two identical springs, each with k = 60 N/m, are both stretched by 0.15 m. Calculate the total elastic potential energy stored in both springs.
silver.question: Two identical springs, each with k = 60 N/m, are both stretched by 0.15 m. Calculate the total elastic potential energy stored in both springs.

guided_steps.say: Elastic PE per spring: \(E_{pe} = \frac{1}{2}ke^2\). Then add both springs.

guided_steps.done: 0.675 J per spring, so the total is 1.35 J.

misconceptions.message: Each spring stores ½ × 60 × 0.15² = 0.675 J. Two springs store 0.675 × 2 = 1.35 J. 0.675 J is only one spring.
Square the extension: 0.15² = 0.0225. Skipping the square gives ½ × 60 × 0.15 × 2 = 9.0 J.
